```{r load}
# data from data-raw/vignette_method.R, the methodology article's bundle
vd <- function(f) system.file("vignette-data", f, package = "knowledge", mustWork = TRUE)
x <- readRDS(vd("method.rds"))
reg <- x$settings
pk <- x$picks
sc <- as.data.frame(x$scope)
val <- function(key) gsub(";", ", ", reg$value[reg$key == key], fixed = TRUE)
n0 <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
issue <- function(n) sprintf("[#%s](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/knowledge/issues/%s)", n, n)
species <- c(BT = "bull trout", CH = "chinook", CO = "coho", GR = "grayling", ST = "steelhead",
             WCT = "westslope cutthroat trout")
key_words <- function(k) {
  paste(species[[sub("_.*$", "", k)]], if (grepl("_rear$", k)) "rearing" else "spawning")
}
words_and <- function(v) if (length(v) < 2) v else paste(paste(v[-length(v)], collapse = ", "), "and", v[length(v)])
sc$share <- sc$groups_both / sc$groups
sc$margin <- sc$null_heldout_curve - sc$dev_curve
under_half <- sc$key[sc$share < 0.5]
withheld <- sc$key[sc$grade_withheld]
# a key whose curve failed has no margin and no grade, and the run's flag for it reads FALSE
curved <- sc[!is.na(sc$margin), ]
closest <- curved[which.min(abs(curved$margin)), ]
# the words: the table holds every published key (the bundle's gradient limits come from data/thresholds.csv); every
# published key drops some groups, and more than half for the keys named; the gate withholds some
# keys and publishes others, and its closest call is decided by less than one unit of deviance. A bundle without
# `scope` would make every comparison logical(0), which stopifnot() passes
stopifnot(nrow(sc) > 0, setequal(sc$key, x$site_gradient$limits$key), all(sc$groups_both < sc$groups),
          length(under_half) >= 2,
          length(withheld) >= 1, any(!is.na(sc$margin) & !sc$grade_withheld), nrow(closest) == 1,
          abs(closest$margin) < 1, abs(closest$margin) >= 0.05,
          # the caption's sign: at zero or above withheld, below published (away from a tie the summary's rounding
          # could blur)
          with(curved[abs(curved$margin) > 1e-3, ], identical(grade_withheld, margin <= 0)),
          # the settings the prose quotes
          identical(val("prior_sd"), "2.5"), identical(val("se_region"), "1"), identical(val("folds"), "5"))
```


The tuning chooses the thresholds of a fish habitat definition, the few limits on a stream's size and slope that say
where a species spawns or rears, from the Province's fish sampling records, and grades each stream by how often the
species is caught on streams like it. Two textbooks set out how such a choice is made well: *Statistical Rethinking*
[@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking] and *Bayesian Data Analysis* [@gelman_etal2013Bayesiandata]. This article reads
the tuning against them: what it does as they teach, where it departs and why, and what we test next. It is a record
of where the method stands and where it is heading; the [methodology article](tuning-method.html) sets out its steps.

**The answer.** The tuning judges habitat definitions the way *Statistical Rethinking* teaches: on watershed groups
left out of the fit, telling two apart by the uncertainty of their difference, and keeping the near-ties together
rather than naming one winner. Its three main departures are each defensible for a habitat definition whose job is to
rank streams. The score measures how well a habitat definition ranks streams within a watershed group, not how often
the species turns up in a new one; the prior is used as a penalty that finds one best value, not a full posterior; and
the thresholds are reported as one choice and a range, not a distribution. Three things should change: a check on how
the choice is made does not fully hold its test data out, the two models the publishing test compares treat a site
from an unfamiliar data set or period differently, and the stream slopes the habitat definitions read depend on where
fish were caught.

## What does the tuning do? {#tuning}

For each species and life stage, the tuning builds a grid of habitat definitions around those of
[`link`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/link/) [@link], the R package that maps habitat on BC's streams: a
floor on stream size, a ceiling on slope, and for some an exception for small streams near a large river. Each habitat
definition sorts every site crews electrofished into habitat or not.

The **scorer** is a regression of whether the species was caught at a site on that sorting. Beside it sit the area
fished (the effort) and two **sampling terms**, the data set the record comes from and its period, which are
differences in how crews sampled that a habitat definition must not be credited for. Each watershed group the scorer
keeps (the Province divides its streams into these large drainages) also gets its own **base rate**: how often the
species is caught there, other things equal. The **score** is the scorer's deviance at sites in watershed groups left
out when the habitat definition, effort and sampling terms were fitted, a measure of how badly it predicts the catch,
summed over sites; lower is better. (Each left-out group's base rate is then fitted on its own sites, as the next
sections explain.)

The groups are dealt into `r val("folds")` **folds**, and each fold in turn is left out of the fit and scored. Habitat
definitions whose scores lie within one standard error of their difference from the best are **close calls**, and
among them we choose the one that changes `link`'s current habitat definition least. Then a second model, the **curve**, a smooth surface of how often the
species is caught against stream size, distance to a river and slope, gives every stream the species can reach that
has a size and a slope a **grade**. The **gate**
publishes those grades only if the curve scores better on the left-out folds than no habitat definition at all.

## The checks, at a glance {#glance}

Each row is one question the books raise, what the tuning does, and where that leaves it. The sections below take
them in turn.

```{r glance}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  question = c(
    "Is the score taken on data the fit did not see?",
    "Are two scores told apart by the uncertainty of their difference?",
    "Does the score predict a new watershed group?",
    "How wide is a close call, and which close call is chosen?",
    "Does the check on the choosing hold its test data out?",
    "Is the prior a regularising prior at Bayesian Data Analysis's default scale?",
    "Does the prior give a posterior?",
    "Are thresholds reported as a distribution?",
    "Are watershed groups pooled?",
    "Which watershed group does the grade describe?",
    "Is the gate a fair comparison?",
    "Is an unfamiliar data set or period read the same on both sides of the gate?",
    "Is the catch rate per square metre the same however much area is fished?",
    "Is a miss an absence?",
    "Are the inputs measured?",
    "Is a stream's slope independent of the catch?"),
  `what the tuning does` = c(
    "Whole watershed groups are left out of each fit and scored",
    "Yes: the standard error of each difference, over watershed groups",
    "No: each left-out group's base rate is refitted first",
    "One standard error; the close call nearest link's current habitat definition",
    "Not fully: the scores it chooses from were fitted with its test groups in",
    "Yes, scale 2.5, but normal not Cauchy, complementary log-log not logit, and on the sampling terms only",
    "No: it is fitted as a penalty, which finds one best value",
    "No: as one choice and the range of close calls",
    "Fixed in the scorer, with groups of one outcome dropped; pooled in the curve",
    "An average group",
    "A point comparison against no habitat definition, with no standard error",
    "No: the scorer takes the reference level, the curve the most common one",
    "Not necessarily: the area fished has a fitted slope, so the rate per square metre can change with area",
    "A miss is read as no catch at that visit",
    "No: placement, slope and flow are estimates read as exact",
    "No: link cuts streams at fish records"),
  verdict = c("follows the books", "follows the books", "departs, defensibly", "departs", "should change",
              "follows the books", "departs, defensibly", "departs, defensibly", "departs", "follows the books",
              "departs", "should change", "departs, defensibly", "departs", "departs", "should change"),
```

## Is the score an honest test? {#score}

A model judged on the data it was fitted to always looks better than it is: the honest test is data it has not seen.
When the data come in clusters, *Statistical Rethinking* separates two tests:

> "If we wish to validate a model against the specific clusters used to fit the model, that is one thing. But if we instead wish to compute predictions for new clusters, other than the ones observed in the sample, that is quite another." [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 426]

The tuning leaves out whole watershed groups, the strict form, so no site in a scored group helped estimate how much
the habitat definition, the effort or the sampling terms matter. But before a left-out group is scored, the scorer
refits that group's base rate on that group's own sites. So the score asks whether the habitat definition puts the
catches on the right streams within a group, not how many catches a new group would hold. Every habitat definition
gets the same refit, one fitted value per group, so by our reasoning (not measured) each is flattered by about the
same amount: the comparison between habitat definitions holds, while the score itself is not a prediction for a new
group. That is the right question for a habitat definition that ranks streams, since how common a species is in a
watershed is not the habitat definition's to predict. The score is also taken at one best estimate, where the books
average it over the posterior [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 210; @gelman_etal2013Bayesiandata, p. 174].

## How are two habitat definitions told apart? {#se}

Two scores are close or far by the uncertainty of their difference, not of each score alone:

> "we don’t use their standard errors but rather the standard error of their difference." [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 227]

The tuning takes the standard error (SE) of each habitat definition's difference from the best over watershed groups,
the units it leaves out, as the book does over sites [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 228]. Every habitat
definition within `r val("se_region")` SE of the best is a close call, and the published table gives the range of
close calls beside the choice, closer to what the book asks than a single winner [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking,
p. 225]. The width of one SE is a convention neither book sets, and choosing the close call nearest `link`'s current
habitat definition is a decision the scores do not make.

Choosing among thousands of habitat definitions also flatters the winner's score. *Bayesian Data Analysis* warns that
when scores like these are used to choose a model, "the predictive performance estimate of the selected model is biased due to the selection process" [@gelman_etal2013Bayesiandata, p. 182],
and names the remedy, a second level of left-out data. The tuning's check on the choosing (choosing on four folds and
scoring the choice on the fifth) was meant to be that, but the scores it chooses from came from fits that included
the fifth fold, so its test data were not fully left out. The check reports on the choosing only; it moves no choice
and no grade.

## What does the prior do? {#prior}

A regularising prior is sceptical: it slows how fast a model learns from the sample, and keeps an estimate finite
where the data alone would let it run away. Where one data set or period caught the species every time, or never,
its sampling term ran without bound. The tuning gives the sampling terms a normal prior with a standard deviation of
`r val("prior_sd")` on the scorer's complementary log-log scale. A scale of 2.5 is what *Bayesian Data Analysis* uses
for its default prior on logistic regression coefficients, there a Cauchy prior on every coefficient but the constant
[@gelman_etal2013Bayesiandata, p. 416].

The prior is fitted as a penalty, which finds the single most probable value and no more:

> "Ridge regression does not compute a posterior distribution." [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 216]

So the tuning carries no uncertainty from the prior into its thresholds, which it reports as one choice and the range
of close calls, and no simulation of what the prior implies for the catch has been run
[@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 328]. The scorer also keeps a fallback, a fit without the prior, for a
fold whose usual fit would lose a term; by the way the prior is built the sampling terms cannot send a fold there, but
that rests on an argument, not a check.

## Are watershed groups pooled? {#pooling}

A model can give each watershed group its own base rate, learned from that group alone, or let the groups share what
they have in common, so a group with few sites borrows from the rest. The second, partial pooling, helps most where a
group has little data:

> "Smaller ponds produce more error, but the partial pooling estimates are better on average, especially in smaller ponds." [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 413]

The scorer gives each watershed group its own base rate, which is cheap enough to score thousands of habitat
definitions and answers the within-group question above. But a group whose sites all caught the species, or none did,
has a base rate that runs to the edge and says nothing about the habitat definition, so it is dropped. For
`r words_and(vapply(under_half, key_words, ""))`, more than half the groups are dropped. The curve does pool the
groups: it learns a spread of base rates across them. But it is fitted on at most the groups the scorer keeps, and
each left-out group is still scored by its own refitted base rate, so the pooled spread is never used to predict a
group the curve has not seen.

```{r scope}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `species and stage` = vapply(sc$key, key_words, ""),
  `watershed groups with sites` = n0(sc$groups),
  `kept by the scorer (catches and misses)` = n0(sc$groups_both),
  `grade` = ifelse(is.na(sc$margin), "no curve", ifelse(sc$grade_withheld, "withheld", "published")),
  `curve's deviance less no habitat definition's` = ifelse(is.na(sc$margin), "", sprintf("%.1f", -sc$margin)),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = paste("The watershed groups each species and stage's sites fall in, the groups the scorer keeps, and",
                  "whether its grade is published. The last column is the curve's deviance on the left-out folds",
                  "less that of no habitat definition: below zero the curve does better, and at zero or above its",
                  "grade is withheld."),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrlr")
```

The grade describes an average group, leaving each group's own base rate out [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking,
p. 428], which is the right reading for a map that compares streams across the province. But because every score
refits each group's base rate, no score has tested how well the grade compares a stream in one group with a stream in
another.

## Is the gate a fair comparison? {#gate}

The gate compares the curve's deviance on the left-out folds with that of no habitat definition, on the same sites and
folds. This is the comparison the books teach, and it does not need to charge the curve again for its flexibility,
because the curve's smoothness is already penalised as it is fitted. But it is a point comparison with no standard
error, so any improvement publishes, and the curve's variables come from the choice made on the same folds. It
withholds `r words_and(vapply(withheld, key_words, ""))`. Its closest call, `r key_words(closest$key)`, was
`r if (closest$grade_withheld) "withheld" else "published"` by `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(closest$margin))` in deviance.

The two sides of the gate also differ at one kind of site. Where a left-out site comes from a data set or period the
fit never saw, the no-habitat-definition side, which runs through the scorer, gives it the reference level, the
prior's centre; the curve gives it the most common level in the fit. So the two sides treat that site differently.

## What else differs? {#else}

- **Effort is fitted, not fixed.** The area fished enters with a fitted slope rather than as a fixed exposure (an
  offset), so the catch rate per square metre fished can rise or fall with the area fished: the hypothesis
  *Statistical Rethinking* describes for a free coefficient on the log of exposure
  [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 357]. Electrofishing a larger area plausibly catches less per square
  metre.
- **A miss is a miss at that visit.** The response is whether a crew caught the species on one visit, so a species
  present and missed reads as absent [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 499]. The grade says so: it is expected
  use per standard electrofishing visit, not habitat quality. Telling the two apart needs repeat visits.
- **The inputs are carried as exact.** A site's place on the stream, its slope and its modelled flow are each
  estimates. The tuning drops the worst-placed sites and reads the rest as measured, where the book carries such
  error into the model [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 495].
- **A stream's slope depends on the catch.** `link` cuts streams at fish records, so a site that caught fish sits on
  a shorter stretch, and the slope the habitat definitions read depends on what was caught.

## What do we test next? {#next}

- **Three fixes to the tuning** (`r issue(203)`): the curve gives a site from an unfamiliar data set or period the
  reference level, as the scorer does; a run stops if the scorer ever fits a fold without its prior, so that rests on
  a check; and the check on the choosing is either nested, each fold's choice made from fits that never saw it, or
  described as what it is.
- **A pooled curve, scored both ways** (`r issue(186)`), for chinook and westslope cutthroat trout rearing: a full
  posterior with priors on the smooths, and the groups with only catches or only misses kept. Today's curve and the
  pooled one are each scored both by every left-out group's own refitted base rate and as a new group drawn from the
  spread of groups, since a new-group score for one beside an own-base-rate score for the other compares nothing. Two
  cheap tests ride with it: the area fished as a fixed exposure, and a simulation of what the prior implies for the
  catch.
- **Slopes that do not depend on the catch** (`r issue(70)`): modelled slopes checked against field-measured ones,
  and slopes over fixed lengths of stream scored beside `link`'s segment slope.

## What this review did not test {#limits}

- It reads the method and fits nothing; how much each change moves a score is measured by the work that makes it.
- Occupancy models, which separate a missed species from an absent one, are named in *Statistical Rethinking* but
  not taught there, and penalised splines are named in *Bayesian Data Analysis* without the smoothing library's
  penalty scale, so this review stops at what the books say.
- It describes the code at commit `r x$meta$commit` and the run whose summaries this article's data, written on
  `r x$meta$written`, read.
